topic: News breakdown: Meta removes the AI "train" clause from its new business terms after publisher backlash
post:
Meta just deleted one word from its business terms: "train." ✂️
Here's why that one word set off newsrooms everywhere.

What happened 👇
📄 Meta's new commercial terms take effect October 30, and apply to businesses with a Meta account
⚖️ Three legal experts told Nieman Lab the original wording could be read to let Meta crawl news sites and use that content to train its AI
🚫 There was no opt-out: keep using Meta's business tools, and you accept the terms

Then the backlash.
Meta first called the reports "false." Then it removed the sentence about using crawled content to "train" its products, and said the crawling covers advertising and business products.

But the crawling permission itself stays. Meta says website owners can still use robots.txt to set what crawlers can access. The News/Media Alliance called the change a step in the right direction, but said it's not enough.

Why it matters:
The AI data fight is moving from lawsuits into the fine print. One sentence in a terms update can decide whose content trains the next model. 🔍

Practical takeaway:
If your company runs a website, check your robots.txt this week, and read the next terms update before you click "accept." 📝

Should platforms need clear permission before using your content for AI? 👇
